title: When a Forecast Needs More Room — Robert Engle’s (1982) U.K. Inflation ARCH Variance Equations & Tim Bollerslev’s (1986) Persistent GARCH(1,1) Conditional Volatility Forecasting

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: Calm months cluster together and turbulent months cluster together—so forecast error bars shouldn't stay the same width all year. Engle's ARCH and Bollerslev's GARCH let forecast variance expand after big surprises and gradually relax during quiet stretches.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Assuming constant volatility blinds inflation forecasters, power-grid planners, and risk managers right when big shocks hit back-to-back.
keyTakeaways: Robert Engle (1982) modeled U.K. inflation uncertainty by making today's conditional variance depend on squared recent forecast errors (ARCH).
Tim Bollerslev (1986) added yesterday's conditional variance itself to create GARCH(1,1), parsimoniously capturing long volatility persistence with just three parameters.
When alpha + beta approaches 1, a single large shock widens prediction intervals for many periods before reverting toward baseline variance.

vocab.meaning: Time-varying forecast variance that depends on recent history, even if long-run unconditional variance is finite.
Mandelbrot's observation that large changes tend to be followed by large changes (of either sign), and small by small.
Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity: sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha * epsilon_{t-1}^2 + beta * sigma_{t-1}^2.

quiz.question: In a GARCH(1,1) model sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha * e_{t-1}^2 + beta * sigma_{t-1}^2, what condition keeps long-run unconditional variance positive and finite?
options: omega > 0, alpha >= 0, beta >= 0, and alpha + beta < 1
quiz.explanation: Non-negative weights keep variance positive, and alpha + beta < 1 ensures shocks eventually decay toward omega / (1 - alpha - beta).
